title: The School Shop
big_idea: Make a plan that fits a budget, and list every way to be sure.
child_idea: A budget is the money you have. Choose what to buy so that it fits, find the total and the change, and list every way in order so that none is missed.

moe.strand: Money applied: total, change and choosing within a budget (Primary 1)
topics: Money in dollars up to $100; addition and subtraction within 100 in money stories (Primary 1, p. 31)
Which two items cost exactly a given amount (a Primary 1 paper item), cost of several equal items, how much is left
Listing every way to make an exact amount (a systematic list, contest-style): beyond Primary 1
moe.note: Strand label for the tutor only. BEYOND PRIMARY 1 ON PURPOSE at Think harder and Go further only. Start here is Primary 1 money work: which two tags cost exactly $10 (the 'which two items did he buy' item appears in several Primary 1 papers), the total of two items, how much is left, whether $10 is enough, the cost of 3 equal items and a table of had, spent and left. Think harder: every way to spend exactly $20 on two items ('Exactly $20', a table with a row for each number of books), is a list complete, three items and change from $50, and true or false on a list of ways (the same way in a different order is not a new way). Go further: every way to pay $20 with $2, $5 and $10 notes (6 ways), a puzzle with 7 things and an exact total, and writing an 'exactly' puzzle for a partner. Listing every way is not a Primary 1 outcome (it is contest-style and sits at Think harder by owner decision 6). Owner decision, 22 and 23 Oct 2026: strong content with scaffolding, said plainly to families; every lesson names a beyond item. Do not describe the lesson as MOE-aligned. Money wording follows the Primary 1 paper patterns: dollars as $12, whole dollars only, no $20 note (a $20 payment is two ten-dollar notes), cashier, change, 'how much is left'. Non-routine types (tutor only): how many ways, systematic list with a check, guess and check, true or false on a list.

contest_moves: how many ways: every way to spend exactly $20 (a table with a row for each number of books)
systematic list with a check that no case is missing: is this list complete
guess and check: which two items cost exactly this much; 7 things for exactly $20
the same way in a different order is not a new way (true or false)
contest_where: Think harder, Go further and the Investigation
objectives: Choose two tags that cost exactly a given amount, and say whether a budget is enough.
Find the total of two or three items, the cost of 3 equal items, and the money left or the change.
List every way to pay an exact amount by working in order (start with the most expensive item and go down), so that no way is missed or repeated.
Think harder: every way to spend exactly $20 on two items, whether a list is complete, three items and change from $50.
Go further: every way to pay $20 with $2, $5 and $10 notes, 7 things for an exact total, and writing an exactly-puzzle.

remember: What goes with 7 to make 10 (Term 1 Lesson 5, taught again with a ten-frame)
Three of the same price, by adding again and again (Term 2 Lesson 15, taught again with three tags)
List every pair that makes 6, starting at 1 (Term 2 Lesson 17, taught again with a table)
joining_cold.assumes: Only counting to 20 and the price tags and play money from the lessons before. Nothing from the lessons before is needed: the warm-up makes 10 on a ten-frame, adds three equal prices and lists pairs that make 6 in order. The words budget, exactly, total, left and change are taught in Explore and the Mini-lesson.
joining_cold.note: Fairly safe to miss: this lesson applies Lessons 24 and 25. Mi's Challenge Quest has a gate on this idea (two items that cost exactly an amount), so a child who misses it watches the recording and does workbook pages 1 and 2 before the Quest. A child who joins here cold can follow: the warm-up makes 10, adds equal prices and lists in order, and Start here keeps to totals within $20.

child: The price tags from the lesson before (9 with a price, 3 blank), kept in their envelope
The play money from Term 3 Lesson 4 (notes and coins), kept in its envelope
No tags or money? Small pieces of paper with a price written on each one
A pencil, a rubber and spare paper
tutor: Your own price tags and play money to show on camera, if you wish
kit_pages: No new kit page this lesson. Keep the price tags and the play money in their envelope (the money and the tags come back in the Quest).
materials.notes: No ruler is needed. Nothing needs to be bought. The money is PLAY MONEY, not real money. Small pieces stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears; keep them away from younger brothers and sisters. No matches, toothpicks or anything sharp. Nobody cuts during the lesson. A way that needs more than five $2 notes is written down, not laid out.

kit_contract.piece: price tags with a price (from the lesson before)

timing.notes: Opening is 2 minutes. Explore has 11 minutes: two tags that make exactly $12 (and how to be sure there are only two), then every way to make $10 with $2 and $5 notes. The mini-lesson has 11: is the money enough, the cost of 3 equal items, a table that lists every way to pay $12 and total then change. The workbook has 32 minutes: Start here takes a middle child about 17 minutes, so pages 3 to 5 are for home for most children. The last 5 minutes are the standing buffer.
skip_order: Start with: shorten Explore round 3 (what did we notice) to one question
Then: take the extra minutes from the flex time

sneak_peek.q1: Mei buys a pencil for $3 and a rubber for $2. How much does she pay altogether? Write the number.
sneak_peek.q2: Kumar has exactly $9. He buys two things. The tags say $2, $4, $5 and $7. Which two does he buy? I know because ___.
sneak_peek.a2: $2 and $7, or $4 and $5. Both pairs make $9: 2 and 7 make 9, and 4 and 5 make 9.

slides.title: The School Shop

blocks.head: TODAY WE WILL
items: Plan what to buy, and list every way.

slides.note: Lesson 6 of Term 3, 90 minutes. Objective: choose items that make an exact amount or fit a budget, find the total and the change, and list every way in order so that none is missed. Plain statement for families: which two items cost exactly an amount, the total, the change and the cost of equal items are Primary 1 work; listing every way to make an amount, and paying with three kinds of note, go past the school Primary 1 syllabus on purpose. Time plan: opening 0 to 2, warm-up 2 to 8, sneak-peek 8 to 12, explore 12 to 23, mini-lesson 23 to 34, brain break 34 to 38, workbook 38 to 70, talk 70 to 76, exit ticket 76 to 82, look-back 82 to 85, flex time and goodbye 85 to 90 (the buffer: do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose. Say the recording notice in one line: the recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted; a child may keep the microphone and camera off.
slides.subtitle: A plan that fits the money

mascot.say: Hi, I'm Mi. Let's notice, test and explain why!

slides.title: Warm-up: make 10

blocks.text: 7 are filled. How many more make 10?

slides.note: A ten-frame with 7 counters (Term 1 Lesson 5, taught again). Ask: how many more make 10 (3). Say: 7 and 3 make 10. Today we look for two prices that make an exact amount, so we need the partner of a number. A child who is unsure counts the empty squares. Children answer aloud. No writing.

slides.title: Three of the same

blocks.text: 3 pens at $4 each. How much do they cost altogether?

slides.note: Three of the same price (Term 2 Lesson 15, taught again as adding again and again): 4 and 4 and 4. Ask: how much do 3 pens cost altogether (12). Add two at a time: 4 and 4 make 8, 8 and 4 make 12. A child who is unsure uses three groups of 4 fingers. Children answer aloud. No writing.

slides.title: List every pair that makes 6

blocks.text: Start at 1 and go up. Stop when the numbers swap round.

slides.note: Listing in order (Term 2 Lesson 17, taught again). Start at 1: 1 and 5. Then 2 and 4. Then 3 and 3. After that the pairs swap round (4 and 2 is the same pair as 2 and 4), so we stop. Say: starting at the smallest and going up in order means we do not miss one. Ask for the second and third rows. Answers: 4; 3 and 3. A child who is unsure counts on fingers from the first number to 6. Children answer aloud. No writing.

slides.title: Sneak-peek puzzles

blocks.text: Ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start. Nobody is marked.

cols.head: PUZZLE 1: anyone can try
items: Mei buys a pencil for $3.
She buys a rubber for $2.
How much does she pay altogether?

cols.head: PUZZLE 2: think
items: Kumar has exactly $9. He buys two things.
The tags say $2, $4, $5 and $7.
Which two does he buy? I know because ___.

slides.note: Puzzle 1 (3 and 2: $5) is an access question. Puzzle 2 is a thinking question on the lesson idea: two tags that make exactly $9. There are two answers: $2 and $7, and $4 and $5. A child who finds one has done well; ask if there is another. Say: two sneak-peek puzzles, ideas we have not learnt yet; a guess is a great start and I do not know is welcome; nobody is marked. Children write on their own paper. Nobody holds paper to the camera. There is no private chat. Answers: $5; $2 and $7, or $4 and $5. Do not reveal puzzle 2 until Talk time. Do not write scores or keep a list.

slides.title: Explore: exactly $12

items: Take the rubber, pencil, pen, glue, ruler and cup tags.
Find two different tags that cost exactly $12 together.
There are two answers. How do you know you have them all?

slides.note: Round 1, about 5 minutes. Each child lays out six tags: rubber $2, pencil $3, pen $4, glue $5, ruler $7 and cup $8. They find two tags that cost exactly $12 together. There are two answers: pen $4 and cup $8, and glue $5 and ruler $7. Ask: how do you know you have them all? Model the way to be sure: start with the tag that costs the least and ask what partner it needs. Rubber $2 needs $10 (no tag); pencil $3 needs $9 (no tag); pen $4 needs $8 (the cup, yes); glue $5 needs $7 (the ruler, yes); the ruler and cup are already found. The prices are on the tags, so the slide shows no price. The answer appears on the next slide. A child with no tags writes the prices 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 on paper. Answers: $4 and $8, $5 and $7.

slides.title: Two ways to make $12

blocks.text: $4 and $8. $5 and $7. Start with the tag that costs the least and ask what partner it needs.

slides.note: The answers for round 1: $4 and $8 (pen and cup), and $5 and $7 (glue and ruler). Say: starting with the tag that costs the least and asking what it needs means we do not miss one. Children check against their own tags and tick. Nobody holds tags up to the camera: children say the pair and show a thumb when they agree.

slides.title: Explore: pay exactly $10

items: Take your $2 notes and your $5 notes.
Pay exactly $10 using only $2 notes and $5 notes.
How many different ways can you find?

slides.note: Round 2, about 5 minutes. Children use the play-money notes: five $2 notes and four $5 notes (they need at most five of one and two of the other). They find every way to pay exactly $10 with $2 notes and $5 notes. There are two ways: five $2 notes, or two $5 notes. Ask for each way, then: how do you know there are only two? Try one $5 note: $5 is left, and $2 notes cannot make $5 exactly. Children say the way and show a thumb; nobody holds notes up. A child with no notes draws or writes 2s and 5s on paper. The pictures are on the next slide.

slides.title: Two ways to pay $10

blocks.text: Five $2 notes, or two $5 notes. One $5 note leaves $5 and $2 notes cannot make that.

slides.note: The answers for round 2: five $2 notes, or two $5 notes. Say: a $5 note on its own leaves $5, and $2 notes make 2, 4, 6, so $5 cannot be made. Children tick their own work.

slides.title: What did we notice?

items: How did you know there were only two ways?
Why start with the tag that costs the least, or the biggest note?
Is 5 two-dollar notes then 2 five-dollar notes a new way, or the same two ways in a different order?

slides.note: Take one or two answers from volunteers. Key ideas: working in order (the tag that costs the least first, or the biggest note first) means no way is missed; checking what is left shows when a way is impossible; the same pieces in a different order is the same way. Repeat a child answer in your own words so the recording picks it up. Do not give the rule before the children say it.

slides.title: Is the money enough?

blocks.text: Mei has $15. Does she have enough for the toy car and the shoe? Circle Yes or No on your paper.

slides.note: Worked example. Mei has $15. The toy car costs $11 and the shoe costs $6. Ask: how much do they cost altogether (17); is $17 more than $15 (yes); so is $15 enough (No). How much more money does she need (2)? Say: a budget is the money you have. Enough means the total is the same as the budget or less. Children answer aloud. The answer is on the next slide. A child who says Yes because both prices are less than 15 forgot to add: ask what altogether means.

slides.title: Not enough: she needs $2 more

blocks.text: $11 + $6 = $17. $17 is more than $15. No, $15 is not enough.
Mei needs $2 more.

slides.note: The answer: the car and the shoe cost $17, which is more than $15, so $15 is not enough and Mei needs $2 more (15 up to 17). Say: enough means the total is not more than the money you have.

slides.title: Three of the same

blocks.text: Ravi buys 3 glue sticks. How much do they cost altogether?

slides.note: Three glue sticks at $5 each. Ask: how much altogether (15): 5 and 5 make 10, and 5 more make 15. Say it as a number sentence: $5 + $5 + $5 = $15. The answer is on the next slide. Then ask a second one aloud: a rubber costs $2 and Siti buys 5; how much (10). Children write the second on their own paper. A child who writes 5 gave one price: ask how many glue sticks.

slides.title: Add the same price again

blocks.text: $5 + $5 + $5 = $15. Ravi pays $15 altogether.

slides.note: The answers: $15 for 3 glue sticks and $10 for 5 rubbers at $2. Read them aloud and children tick their own work. Say: the same price added again and again.

slides.title: Every way to pay $12

blocks.text: Pay exactly $12 with $5 notes and $2 notes. Fill in the last column. Write X if it cannot be done.

slides.note: The table lists every way in order. Start with no $5 notes: $12 is left, and 12 is 6 two-dollar notes (2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12). With one $5 note: $7 is left, and $2 notes cannot make 7 exactly (X). With two $5 notes: $2 is left, which is 1 two-dollar note. A third $5 note would be $15, more than $12, so we stop. Children try the last column on paper first; wait 15 seconds. Answers: 6; X; 1. So there are 2 ways: six $2 notes, or two $5 notes and one $2 note. Six $2 notes is more than the five in the kit: write it, do not lay it out. The filled table is on the next slide.

slides.title: Two ways: the table checks every case

blocks.text: Two ways: six $2 notes, or two $5 notes and one $2 note.

slides.note: The filled table: 6, X, 1. Say: each row is one case, and no case is missed. Two ways: six $2 notes, or two $5 notes and one $2 note. Children tick their own work.

slides.title: Total, then change

blocks.text: Mei buys the cup and the pencil. She gives the cashier two ten-dollar notes. How much change?

slides.note: Two steps. First the total: the cup costs $8 and the pencil costs $3, so they cost $11. Then the change from $20: count up from 11 to 20, which is 9. Ask: how much altogether (11); how much change (9). Children answer aloud. The answer is on the next slide. A child who gives 12 took away only the cup: ask what else she bought.

slides.title: Total first, then count up

blocks.text: $8 + $3 = $11. 11 up to 20 is $9 change.

slides.note: The answers: the total is $11, and the change is $9 (11 up to 20). Say: first the total, then count up to what was paid.

slides.title: Clap and stamp

blocks.text: Stand up. Clap for a two-dollar note. Stamp for a five-dollar note.
Make each amount: $7 is stamp, clap.
Sip some water.

slides.note: Four minutes. Stand up on camera with a little clear space. Call an amount and children make it with claps ($2 each) and stamps ($5 each): $7 is one stamp and one clap, $9 is a stamp and two claps, $4 is two claps, $10 is two stamps (or five claps). Then call $6, $11 and $14. No equipment, no running. A child may stay seated and tap the desk softly. Do not give prizes or compare children.

slides.title: Workbook page 1: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 1 to 3. Take your time.

slides.note: Read questions 1 to 3 aloud. Children work on their own; the tutor walks the cameras and asks how do you know. Wait 10 seconds before helping. After question 3 any child may choose to carry on or try Think harder. Question 1: four tags, which two cost exactly $10. Question 2: a ruler $7 and a cup $8, how much altogether. Question 3: Wei has $20 and buys a jar for $14; how much is left.

slides.title: Check page 1
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children tick their own page with a tick. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q1 $3 and $7; Q2 $15; Q3 $6.

slides.title: Workbook page 2: Start here

blocks.text: Questions 4 to 6. Take your time.

slides.note: Read questions 4 to 6 aloud. Question 4: Ali has $10; a ruler costs $7 and a glue stick costs $5; enough or not, and how much more. Question 5: 3 rulers at $7. Question 6: a table of money had, spent and left. Wait 10 seconds before helping.

slides.title: Check page 2
slides.note: Read each answer aloud so a child watching the recording can tick their own work. Never ask a child to show a wrong answer to the group. Answers: Q4 No, $2 more; Q5 $7 + $7 + $7 = $21; Q6 8, 9 and 17.

slides.title: Choose your next page

rows: Exactly $20, is the list complete, three items and change
Three kinds of note, 7 things, your own puzzle
Finish and check your own work

blocks.text: Everyone may choose. Not finished? Pages 3 to 5 are for home too.

slides.note: Invite the whole group at once, for example: when you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation. Never announce who is on which page and never name a child. Pairs are not split unless both children agree. Model answers are in the tutor guide. About 5 minutes.

slides.title: Talk and explain

blocks.head: TWO CHILDREN SAY
items: Ben wants a pen and a book.
One child: buying the pen then the book is a different way from buying the book then the pen.
Another child: it is the same way.

blocks.text: Who is right? How do you know?
I think ... because ...

slides.note: One minute of talk to the grown-up next to you, or to your screen. Volunteers first; a pass is always fine; never call a child by name to answer. Model answer: the second child is right. A way is what you buy, not the order you pick it up: a pen and a book cost the same either way, and listing both would count one way twice. Link to Explore: five $2 notes then nothing, or nothing then five $2 notes, is still one way. Repeat each child answer in your own words for the recording. The two children are in another class: no cast name is given the wrong answer.

slides.title: Back to the sneak-peek

blocks.text: Puzzle 1: $5. Puzzle 2: $2 and $7, or $4 and $5.

slides.note: Reveal both puzzles now. Say: many of you wrote a good reason. Do not read out anyone earlier answer. Puzzle 1: 3 and 2 make 5. Puzzle 2: two answers. 2 needs 7 (yes), 4 needs 5 (yes), 5 is already used, 7 is already used. It was the same idea as round 1: start with the one that costs the least and ask what partner it needs.

slides.title: Exit ticket

blocks.text: On your own. No looking back.

slides.note: Children answer on page 5. Read E1, E2 and E3 aloud, and the four options of E1 (the figures on the slide are small). Children tick their own ticket against the next slide. Nobody holds paper to the camera and there is no private chat.

slides.title: Check the exit ticket
slides.note: Read each answer aloud. Children tick their own ticket with a tick. Answers: option 2, $3 and $8; No; $12.

slides.title: Look-back
slides.note: Three minutes. Children tick or write the look-back box on page 5. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out. If a child ticks I am still stuck, a grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp (the number is in the parent summary, never on a slide). You then help in the open session next lesson. Never a direct message to a child. The Next time I will try row is optional.

mascot.say: Take your time. You can pass.

slides.title: Well done, inquirers!

blocks.text: Show a grown-up one thing you found out today.

blocks.head: NEXT LESSON
items: Calendar Detective
Have ready: the calendar page, torn out along the dashed line, with the 7 day cards cut out by a grown-up. The month page is not cut.

slides.note: Say goodbye and thank the grown-ups. Minutes 85 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If you ran late, finish any open item (the look-back). Do not start anything new. Remind families that the next lesson needs the calendar page torn out and its 7 day cards cut out by a grown-up (the month page is not cut), and that the price tags and the play money stay in their envelope for Mi's Challenge Quest in the last lesson of the term. If the whole class is ahead, show the optional slides and use the Spare-time menu from the tutor guide.

slides.title: Go further: pens and rubbers

blocks.text: A pen costs $4 and a rubber costs $2. Ali spends exactly $10.
How many ways can he do it?

slides.note: Optional, only if you are on time. Pens cost $4 and rubbers cost $2, exactly $10. Start with the most pens: 2 pens ($8) and 1 rubber; 1 pen ($4) and 3 rubbers; 0 pens and 5 rubbers. Three ways. Take two answers and move on. This links to Exactly $20 in Think harder.

slides.title: If we have time: pick one

rows: Starting at the smallest number and going up finds every way. Try it for $12.
Pick two tags. Ask for exactly their total.
Show a toy how a table lists every way.

blocks.text: Optional. Everyone may join.

slides.note: Optional Spare-time menu, used only if the whole class is ahead. Pick one or two activities (3 to 5 minutes each); full tutor lines and answers are in the tutor guide. Never start new content and never name who is ahead. Slow down with how do you know rather than rushing on. These minutes come from the flex buffer and are not part of the 90-minute sum.

lines.text: @rec
Hello, inquirers! Pencil ready, and your price tags and play money on the table. Cameras can be on or off, as you like.
This lesson is recorded so a friend who is away can catch up. The recording has me, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted. You may keep your microphone and camera off.
Microphone off until I ask you to speak. To answer, say it with me on three, show fingers, or give a thumbs up. Nobody holds paper up to the camera.
Today we are in the school shop. We plan what to buy with the money we have. And we find every way, so we do not miss one.
Greet the whole group warmly. Do not use children's first names on the recording.

Keep this to two minutes. Say the recording statement and the microphone routine in the same words every lesson, for anyone who joined late. The routine and the four inquirer rules were introduced in the first lesson of Term 1: do not re-teach them.

Plain statement for families when it comes up: which two items cost exactly an amount, the total, the change and the cost of equal items are Primary 1 work; listing every way to make an amount and paying with three kinds of note go beyond Primary 1 on purpose.

New here? Say in one minute: our three rule words (notice it, test it, explain why); a guess is fine and you can always pass; after Start here you may choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody holds paper to the camera. A child without tags or notes writes the prices on small pieces of paper.
@rec
A ten-frame with seven counters filled. Ten squares make ten.
How many more counters make ten?
What goes with eight to make ten? What goes with six?
Three pens, and each pen costs four dollars. We add the same price again.
How much do three pens cost altogether?
Add together: four and four make eight, and four more make twelve. Say it with me.
A list, in order. We find every pair that makes six. Start at one: one and five. Then two and what?
Two and what make six? Then three and what make six?
After three and three, the pairs swap round. So we stop. Starting at the smallest and going in order means we do not miss one.
If a child is unsure of the partner of 7, count the empty squares on the ten-frame. For three pens, use three groups of four fingers. For the list, count on from the first number to six on fingers.
Answers: 3; 12; 4, then 3 and 3. Children answer with a whisper, fingers or hands. Nobody writes. Joining cold: all you need is counting to 20 and the pictures.
@rec
Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked.
Puzzle one. Mei buys a pencil for three dollars. She buys a rubber for two dollars. How much does she pay altogether? Write the number.
Children write the total on their own paper.
Puzzle two. Kumar has exactly nine dollars. He buys two things. The tags say two dollars, four dollars, five dollars and seven dollars. Which two does he buy? I know because blank.
Children write or draw their answer.
Keep your paper. Nobody shows it. We will check our own thinking later, at Talk time.

Puzzle 1 answer: $5. Puzzle 2 answer: $2 and $7, or $4 and $5 (two answers). Look for good ideas to praise later (a child who tried pairs from the tag that costs the least, or found both). Do not write scores or keep a list.
@rec
The tags and the notes are the teachers today. Take the rubber, pencil, pen, glue, ruler and cup tags. Find two different tags that cost exactly twelve dollars together. There are two answers.
Children look for two tags that cost exactly $12. Tutor scans the cameras.
Which two did you find? How do you know you have them all?

Here is a way to be sure. Start with the tag that costs the least, and ask what partner it needs. Two dollars needs ten. No tag. Three needs nine. No tag. Four needs eight: the cup. Five needs seven: the ruler.
Four and eight, and five and seven. Two ways. Starting with the tag that costs the least means we do not miss one.
Round two. Take your two-dollar notes and your five-dollar notes. Pay exactly ten dollars with only two-dollar notes and five-dollar notes. How many ways can you find?
Children make $10 with $2 and $5 notes.
Tell me one way. Is there another way?
Five two-dollar notes, or two five-dollar notes. If you start with one five-dollar note, five dollars is left. Two-dollar notes cannot make five exactly.
What did you notice? How did you know there were only two ways?
We went in order, so we did not miss a way. And the same notes in a different order are the same way, not a new one.
A child who counts a way twice in a different order: say the same notes, so the same way. A child with no notes writes 2 and 5 on paper. A child who cannot find $12: ask which tag needs 8.

Main room only; you cannot see small tags or notes, so ask children to say the pair and to show a thumb. Answers: $4 and $8, $5 and $7; five $2 notes, or two $5 notes. Do not say the rule before the children do.

A budget is the money you have. Mei has fifteen dollars. The toy car costs eleven dollars and the shoe costs six dollars.
How much do they cost altogether? Is fifteen dollars enough? Circle Yes or No on your paper.
Eleven and six make seventeen. Seventeen is more than fifteen, so it is not enough. Mei needs two dollars more.
Your turn. Ali has twelve dollars. A cup costs four dollars and a bag costs nine dollars. Is twelve dollars enough for both? Write Yes or No, and how much more or how much is left.
Children write on their own paper. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Four and nine make thirteen. That is more than twelve, so No. Ali needs one dollar more.
Ravi buys three glue sticks. Each glue stick costs five dollars.
How much do they cost altogether?
Your turn. A rubber costs two dollars. Siti buys five rubbers. How much do they cost altogether? Write the number.
Children write the total. Wait 10 seconds before helping.
Three glue sticks: fifteen dollars. Five rubbers: ten dollars. Tick your own work.
Every way to pay exactly twelve dollars with five-dollar notes and two-dollar notes. We go in order: no five-dollar notes, then one, then two. Fill in the last column. Write X if it cannot be done.
Children fill in the last column on paper. Wait 15 seconds before helping.

No five-dollar notes: twelve left, six two-dollar notes. One five-dollar note: seven left, which two-dollar notes cannot make. Two five-dollar notes: two left, one two-dollar note. So there are two ways.
Two steps. Mei buys the cup for eight dollars and the pencil for three dollars. She gives the cashier two ten-dollar notes.
How much altogether? Then how much change?
Eight and three make eleven. Count up from eleven to twenty: nine dollars change.

If a child adds the budget and the prices, ask: which is the money I have? If a child stops the table after one row, ask what the next row is. If a child writes 7 in the last cell, ask whether two-dollar notes can make seven exactly.

Key words to use every time: budget, enough, exactly, altogether, left, change, cashier, way. Fixed question forms: Does she have enough? How much more money does she need? How much is left? How much change? Do not use decimals. There is no $20 note: twenty dollars is two ten-dollar notes.

Stand up and get a sip of water. Clap for a two-dollar note. Stamp for a five-dollar note. Seven dollars: one stamp and one clap.

How much money does he have left?

Question 1: three dollars and seven dollars. Question 2: fifteen dollars. Question 3: six dollars. Tick your own page with a tick.

start.text: Ben has exactly $10. He buys two different things. Look at the four tags.
start.hint: Start with the tag that costs the least. What partner does it need to make 10?
start.solution: 3 needs 7 to make 10, and there is a $7 tag. 5 needs 5, but there is only one $5 tag and the two things must be different. 8 needs 2, and there is no $2 tag. So the two tags are $3 and $7.
mistakes: Using the $5 tag twice.
Choosing $3 and $5 or $5 and $7 without adding.

start.text: Siti buys a ruler for $7 and a cup for $8. How much does she pay altogether?
start.hint: Altogether means add the two prices. 7 and 3 make 10.
start.solution: 7 and 8: 7 and 3 make 10, and 5 more makes 15. Siti pays $15 altogether.
mistakes: Taking away: 8 take away 7 is 1.
Writing $78 by joining the digits.

start.text: Wei has $20. He buys a jar for $14. How much money does he have left?
start.solution: Count up from 14 to 20. That is 6 steps. Wei has $6 left.
mistakes: Adding 20 and 14.
Writing 14, the price of the jar.

start.text: Ali has $10. A ruler costs $7 and a glue stick costs $5.

parts.text: Does Ali have enough money for both? Circle Yes or No.

start.hint: Add the two prices first. Is the total more than 10?
start.solution: 7 and 5 make 12. 12 is more than 10, so $10 is not enough. Count up from 10 to 12: Ali needs $2 more.
mistakes: Saying Yes because each price is less than 10.
Writing 12 for the money needed.

start.text: A ruler costs $7. Mei buys 3 rulers.
start.hint: Add the same price three times. 7 and 7 make 14.
start.solution: 7 and 7 make 14. 14 and 7 make 21. Mei pays $21 for 3 rulers.
mistakes: Writing 7 or 14 (one or two rulers).
Writing $73 by joining digits.

start.text: Fill in the blanks in the table.
start.hint: Had take away spent is left. Use it the right way round for each row.
start.solution: Ravi: 20 take away 12 is 8. Aisha: she had 15 and has 6 left, so she spent 9. Kumar: he spent 8 and has 9 left, so he had 17.
mistakes: Adding when the question needs take away.
Writing the same number in two rows.

think.text: Exactly $20. Pens cost $2 each and books cost $7 each. Ali spends exactly $20 on pens and books. He may buy 0 books.

parts.text: Fill in the table. Write X if the money cannot be spent exactly or is not enough.

think.hint: For each number of books, work out what is left for pens.
think.solution: 0 books: $20 is left, which is 10 pens. 1 book: $13 is left, and $2 pens cannot make 13 (X). 2 books cost $14. 20 take away 14 is 6, which is 3 pens. 3 books cost $21, which is too much (X). So there are 2 ways: 10 pens, or 2 books and 3 pens.
mistakes: Stopping after the first way.
Counting 2 books and 3 pens and 3 pens and 2 books as two ways.

think.text: A child in another class lists ways to pay exactly $16 with $2 notes and $5 notes. The list says: eight $2 notes.

parts.text: Is the list complete? Circle Yes or No.
A missing way: ____ five-dollar notes and ____ two-dollar notes.

think.answer: No; 2 five-dollar notes and 3 two-dollar notes
think.hint: Try one $5 note, then two $5 notes. What is left each time?
think.solution: One $5 note leaves $11, which $2 notes cannot make. Two $5 notes leave $6, which is 3 two-dollar notes. So the missing way is 2 five-dollar notes and 3 two-dollar notes. Three $5 notes are $15 and leave $1, which cannot be made.
mistakes: Saying Yes because 8 two-dollar notes work.
Writing 2 five-dollar notes and 6 two-dollar notes.

think.text: Ravi buys a book for $9, a hat for $4 and a pen for $2. He pays with a fifty-dollar note.
think.hint: Add the three prices first. Then count up to 50.
think.solution: 9 and 4 make 13. 13 and 2 make 15. Count up from 15 to 20: 5. Then from 20 to 50: 30. 5 and 30 make 35. Ravi gets $35 change.
mistakes: Adding only two of the prices.
Writing 15 as the change.

think.text: Rubbers cost $3 each and pencils cost $4 each. Ali spends exactly $18. Tick True or False.
think.hint: Work out what each way costs. Does it make exactly 18?
think.solution: 6 rubbers cost 18, so it is a way. 2 rubbers and 3 pencils cost 6 and 12, which is 18, so it is a way. The same things in a different order are the same way. 4 rubbers and 2 pencils cost 12 and 8, which is 20, not 18.
mistakes: Saying a different order is a new way.
Not adding the cost of both things.

tf.s: 2 rubbers and 3 pencils is one way.
3 pencils and 2 rubbers is a different way from 2 rubbers and 3 pencils.
4 rubbers and 2 pencils is one way.

go.text: Pay exactly $20 with $10 notes, $5 notes and $2 notes. Write how many of each note. Find every way. Way 1 is shown. Any order of the ways is fine.
go.answer: Six ways: (2, 0, 0), (1, 2, 0), (1, 0, 5), (0, 4, 0), (0, 2, 5), (0, 0, 10) as ten-dollar, five-dollar, two-dollar notes
go.hint: Start with the most $10 notes, then fewer. Then do the same with $5 notes.
go.solution: Two $10 notes. One $10 note leaves $10: two $5 notes, or five $2 notes. No $10 note: four $5 notes, or two $5 notes and five $2 notes, or ten $2 notes. That is 1 and 2 and 3, which is 6 ways.
mistakes: Stopping at the ways with a $10 note.
Counting the same notes in a different order twice.

go.text: Ali buys 7 things. Stickers cost $2 each and pads cost $5 each. He spends exactly $20.
go.hint: Try a number of pads. Then the rest are stickers. Does it make $20?
go.solution: Try 1 pad: 6 stickers cost 12, and 12 and 5 make 17. Too small. Try 2 pads: 5 stickers cost 10, and 10 and 10 make 20. So 5 stickers and 2 pads.
mistakes: Buying 7 of the same thing.
Giving a way with more or fewer than 7 things.

go.text: Write an exactly puzzle for a partner. Choose two of these tags. Many answers are right.
go.answer: Many answers are right: the two prices must add to the amount
go.hint: Pick two prices and add them. That is the amount.
go.solution: For example, the pencil $3 and the cup $8: spend exactly $11 on two things. The two things cost $3 and $8. Check that the two prices add to the amount.
mistakes: Writing an amount that is not the total of two tags.
Choosing the same tag twice.

investigation.title: Amounts you cannot pay
investigation.first: Can you pay exactly $7 with $2 notes and $5 notes?
investigation.text: Mi has lots of $2 notes and $5 notes. Which amounts from $1 to $12 can Mi not pay exactly? Write them.
investigation.answer: First: yes, one $5 note and one $2 note. Mi cannot pay $1 or $3. Every other amount from $2 to $12 can be paid: $2, $4, $5, $6, $7, $8, $9, $10, $11 and $12.
investigation.look_for: A child who tries each amount from $1 up with a list of notes; a child who sees that $1 and $3 are too small to be made; a child who notices that from $4 on every amount works. Credit any clear method. Do not mark a child down for stopping early.
mistakes: Saying $2 or $5 cannot be paid.
Using a note that is more than the amount.

talk.question: Ben wants a pen and a book. One child says: buying the pen then the book is a different way from buying the book then the pen. Another child says: it is the same way. Who is right? How do you know?
talk.answer: The second child is right. A way is what you buy, not the order you pick it up. The pen and the book cost the same either way, so listing both would count one way twice.
talk.look_for: A child who says the things and the cost are the same, or who links it to the same notes in a different order. Not just a name.

exit.text: Mei spends exactly $11 on two things. The tags say $3, $4, $5 and $8. Which two did she buy? Choose the correct answer. Write its number in the bracket.
exit.solution: 3 and 8 make 11. 3 and 4 make 7, 4 and 5 make 9, and 5 and 8 make 13.
mistakes: Choosing (4) $5 and $8 because they are the biggest.
Choosing a pair without adding.

exit.text: Ben has $12. He wants a pen for $6 and a book for $8. Does he have enough money?
exit.solution: 6 and 8 make 14. 14 is more than 12, so $12 is not enough.
mistakes: Saying Yes because each price is less than 12.
Taking away: 8 take away 6 is 2.

exit.text: A cup costs $3. Ali buys 4 cups. How much do the cups cost altogether?
exit.solution: 3 and 3 make 6. 6 and 3 make 9. 9 and 3 make 12.
mistakes: Writing 3 or 7.
Counting only 3 cups.

home_practice.text: Aisha has $10. A rubber costs $3 and a pencil costs $4. Does she have enough money for both? Circle Yes or No. I know because ___.
home_practice.answer: Yes. 3 and 4 make 7, and 7 is less than 10.
home_practice.solution: Add the prices: 3 and 4 make 7. 7 is less than 10, so $10 is enough.

home_practice.text: Lily buys 5 stickers. Each sticker costs $3. How much do the stickers cost altogether? They cost $____ altogether.
home_practice.solution: 3 and 3 make 6, then 9, then 12, then 15. Five stickers cost $15.

home_practice.text: Mei has $20. She buys a cup for $8 and a pen for $5. How much money does she have left? She has $____ left.
home_practice.solution: 8 and 5 make 13. Count up from 13 to 20: 7. Mei has $7 left.

home_practice.text: Pay exactly $18 with $2 notes and $5 notes. Write both ways. Way 1: ____ five-dollar notes and ____ two-dollar notes. Way 2: ____ five-dollar notes and ____ two-dollar notes.
home_practice.answer: 0 five-dollar and 9 two-dollar; 2 five-dollar and 4 two-dollar (either way can come first)
home_practice.solution: No $5 notes: $18 is 9 two-dollar notes. One $5 note leaves $13, which $2 notes cannot make. Two $5 notes leave $8, which is 4 two-dollar notes. Three $5 notes are $15 and leave $3, which cannot be made.
40 is 4 tens, a jump back: 46. 4 is a hop back: 82.

spare_time.note: Optional time, never added to the 90-minute sum. It comes from the 5-minute flex buffer, from slack in the parts, or from the optional Go further slide.
rules: Whole class ahead: use the Spare-time menu in the Flex time and the optional Go further slide. Pick one or two activities; do not start new content.
A few children ahead: they may choose Go further or the Investigation, which are open to everyone. Never label or name a child, and never announce who is ahead.
Never teach anything the next lesson needs. If the class is ahead, slow down: ask 'How do you know?' and let children explain, rather than rushing on.

menu.title: Is it always true?
menu.tutor: Mei says: to find every way, start at the smallest number and go up one at a time. Is that always true? Try it for exactly $12 with $2 notes and $5 notes, then with $3 and $4 items.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Mei says start at the smallest number and go up. Try it for $12 with $2 and $5 notes.
menu.answer: Yes. Going in order means no case is missed. For $12 with $2 and $5 notes: 2 five-dollar notes and 1 two-dollar note, or 6 two-dollar notes.

menu.title: Make a puzzle for your grown-up
menu.tutor: Pick two price tags. Write: spend exactly this much on two things. Give it to your grown-up, then check together by adding the two prices.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Pick two price tags, write their total and ask your grown-up which two tags make it.
menu.answer: No single answer. Check by adding the two prices: they must make the amount.

menu.title: Teach it back
menu.tutor: Pretend your grown-up or a toy has never listed every way. Teach them how a table with a row for each number of five-dollar notes finds every way to pay exactly $12.
menu.rec: Recording: pause. Teach a grown-up how a table finds every way to pay $12 with $5 and $2 notes.
menu.answer: Row 0: $12 left, 6 two-dollar notes. Row 1: $7 left, not possible. Row 2: $2 left, 1 two-dollar note. Each row is one case, so no way is missed.

parent.summary: We planned what to buy in the school shop. Your child chose two tags for an exact amount, found the total and the change, and listed every way to pay. The total, the change and which two items cost exactly an amount are Primary 1 work.
words: exactly: no more and no less
enough: the total is not more than the money you have
left: the money that remains after buying
a way: what you buy, not the order you pick it up
try_home: Pick two items from a leaflet. Ask: how much altogether? With $20, how much is left?
Ask: which two items cost exactly $10? Start with the one that costs the least.
Pay exactly $10 with $2 and $5 notes. How many ways?
ask: How do you know you have every way?
Is it the same way in a different order?
parent.when_stuck: Let your child use the tags and play money and wait 10 seconds before helping. Asking 'What partner does this price need?' works better than giving the answer. Please do not teach a rule; going in order is the method. If the look-back page says 'I am still stuck', photograph it and send it to our business WhatsApp (+65 9880 5962). Photos are kept 90 days after the program ends.
parent.next: Next lesson: Calendar Detective. Online practice: your tutor will share the link. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is not muted; your child may mute and keep the camera off. Please keep the link private.
parent.quote: Go in order, so that no way is missed. The same things in a different order are the same way.
parent.report_line: Your child is learning to plan within a budget and to list every way in order. This week: two items for an exact amount, total and change, and listing every way to pay $12.
parent.term_line: Your child is learning to give a reason, and to read time and money in real life.

Your price tags and play money, kept in their envelope for Mi's Challenge Quest

safeguarding: The price tags and the play money are paper or card. Small pieces stay on the table: nothing goes in the mouth or ears. No matches or toothpicks. Nobody cuts during the lesson; a grown-up cut the pieces beforehand.
This lesson uses the main room only: no breakout rooms, so the tutor sees every camera. A parent sits nearby but does not give answers.

Nobody holds paper, a tag or a note up to the camera: a gallery view shows everyone. Children tick their own work against the answer slide, answer together on a count of three, or show fingers or a thumb for a choice. There is no private chat.

Never read out a child's name with a right or wrong answer. The recording has the tutor, the shared screen and any voice that is unmuted. Children may mute and keep their cameras off. A child's page is never shown.
Movement break: children need a little clear space, soft shoes or socks on a safe floor, no stairs and no running. Clapping and stamping are gentle; a child may stay seated and tap the desk softly.

A child who is still stuck ticks 'I am still stuck' on the look-back page. A grown-up may photograph that page after class and send it to the business WhatsApp only; photos are kept for 90 days after the program ends. The tutor then helps in the open session next lesson. No private messages to children, and no personal phones.
The look-back is never collected in front of the group or read out. A pass is always allowed.
tutor_prep: Solve every workbook question yourself first. Check the answers: S1 $3 and $7; S2 $15; S3 $6; S4 No and $2; S5 $21; S6 8, 9, 17; T1 10, X, 3 and 2 ways; T2 No, 2 five-dollar and 3 two-dollar notes; T3 $15 and $35; T4 True, True, False, False; G1 six ways; G2 5 stickers and 2 pads; I1 $1 and $3.

Tell parents a week before: no new cutting this lesson. The price tags and the play money from the two lessons before must be in their envelope (a way that needs more than five $2 notes is written, not laid out). The next lesson, Calendar Detective, needs the calendar page torn out and its 7 day cards cut out by a grown-up (the month page is not cut).
Have the slides open. Have your own tags and notes to show on camera if you wish. Practise the clap-and-stamp break.

Check the recording captures the tutor and the shared screen. Children video is excluded; any unmuted voice is recorded. Greet the whole group warmly, then start the recording, then say the notice; do not use children's first names on the recording.

Be plain with families: which two items cost exactly an amount, the total, the change and equal items are Primary 1 work; listing every way to make an amount and paying with three kinds of note are beyond Primary 1 on purpose. Do not call the lesson MOE-aligned. Whole dollars only. There is no $20 note: a $20 payment is two ten-dollar notes.
Slides s-m1 to s-m4 keep the answers off the screen while you ask. Read every question with its prices, and the four options of E1, aloud: the figures on the slides are small.

items.q: Pay exactly $16 with $2 notes and $5 notes. How many different ways are there?
items.hint: Go in order: no $5 notes, one, two, and so on until the notes are too much.
steps: No $5 notes: 8 two-dollar notes. Two $5 notes: 3 two-dollar notes.
One $5 note leaves $11 and three leave $1: $2 notes cannot make those.

slips.say: There is more than one way. Start with no $5 notes and go in order.

tpl.q: Pay exactly {t|usd} with $2 notes and $5 notes. How many different ways are there?
tpl.hint: Go in order: no $5 notes, one, two, and so on until the notes are too much.
steps: Try 0, 1, 2 five-dollar notes and so on, until the notes are too much.
Keep a way when the money left is a whole number of $2 notes (an even amount).

items.q: Ali pays exactly $18 with 2 five-dollar notes and some two-dollar notes. How many two-dollar notes?
items.hint: Take the five-dollar notes away first. Then share the rest into $2 notes.

slips.say: 9 two-dollar notes is the way with no five-dollar notes. The question says 2 five-dollar notes.

tpl.q: Ali pays exactly {t|usd} with {b} five-dollar notes and some two-dollar notes. How many two-dollar notes?

items.q: Ali buys 7 things. Stickers cost $2 each and pads cost $5 each. He spends exactly $20. How many pads does he buy?
items.hint: Try a number of pads. The rest are stickers. Does it make $20?
steps: 10 and 10 make 20, and 5 and 2 make 7 things.

slips.say: 7 is all the things. Pads are only some of them.

items.q: A pen costs $8. Mei buys 4 pens and pays with a fifty-dollar note. What change does she get?
items.hint: Find the cost of 4 pens first. Then count up to 50.
steps: 4 pens cost 8 and 8 and 8 and 8, which is $32.

slips.say: 32 is the cost of the pens. The change is what is left of the $50.

items.q: Make an exactly puzzle for a grown-up. Pick two of your price tags and ask which two cost exactly their total. Check by adding.
items.hint: Pick the two tags first, then add their prices.
steps: Write the total of two tags.
Ask: which two tags cost exactly this much?
Check by adding the two prices.
